program_overview.title: AMC 12 Math Competition Prep: Advanced Algebra to the AIME
program_overview.tagline: The whole high school curriculum at contest depth, a worked example every fortnight, the scoring maths that decides when to guess, and a bridge to the 2027 AIME.
program_overview.description:
The AMC 12 is a mathematics contest for high school students run by the Mathematical Association of America (MAA). It is the senior contest in the American Mathematics Competitions series, which also includes the AMC 8 and the AMC 10. Any student in grade 12 or below who is under 19.5 on competition day can sit it. It is held twice a year, as the AMC 12A and then the AMC 12B (in 2026 the dates were 5 November and 13 November). A student may sit one A contest and one B contest, but cannot take the AMC 10 and the AMC 12 on the same date. Registration is done through a school or an approved competition manager, not through us.

The paper has 25 multiple-choice questions, each with five answer choices, and lasts 75 minutes. Calculators are not allowed. Questions start gentle and become much harder towards the end, so a strong student often spends more time on the last ten questions than on the first fifteen.

The scoring shapes strategy. A correct answer earns 6 points, a blank earns 1.5 points and a wrong answer earns 0, so the maximum is 150. That means guessing is not free. A random guess among five choices is worth 6/5 = 1.2 points on average, less than the 1.5 a blank earns, so a blind guess loses points over time. If you can rule out one choice, a guess among four is worth exactly 1.5, break-even. If you can rule out two, a guess among three is worth 2 points, more than a blank. We teach students to make that decision quickly and honestly on every question they cannot finish.

The AMC 12 covers the whole high school curriculum, including trigonometry, advanced algebra and advanced geometry, but never calculus. That is the big difference from the AMC 10, which stops at elementary algebra, basic geometry, elementary number theory and elementary probability. The AMC 12 is also the door to the next contest. From the 2027 AIME, the MAA announced on 26 August 2026 that qualification is a fixed score: 85 or more on the AMC 12 (or 100 or more on the AMC 10), plus other eligibility rules. The AIME is 15 questions, every answer an integer from 000 to 999, taken on computer at Pearson testing centers in the United States and Canada on 5 or 6 February 2027, in two parts: 8 questions in 90 minutes, then 7 questions in 90 minutes, with no return to Part 1. USAJMO and USAMO selection is now based primarily on the AIME score, and AMC scores are no longer a factor. Students outside the US and Canada should check with their competition manager what applies to them.

This course takes eight months. Months 1 and 2 explain how the AMC 12 works, set a diagnostic and build advanced algebra: polynomials and Vieta's formulas, the remainder and factor theorems, functions, exponentials and logarithms, sequences and series. Months 3 and 4 cover trigonometry, complex numbers and advanced number theory. Months 5 and 6 cover counting, probability and advanced geometry, including circles, coordinates, vectors and solids. Months 7 and 8 are contest craft: 75-minute pacing, full-length timed sets of our own original problems, an error log, and an AIME bridge practised under the new two-part split. Every fortnight is built around a fully worked original example so students see exactly how an idea is used under time pressure.

All problems in our materials are written by us. Past AMC papers are published by the MAA, and students may use them on their own, but we never copy or reconstruct contest items. We are independent of the MAA and we promise learning, never scores, AIME qualification or awards.
what_makes_this_different: AMC 12 only: the whole high school curriculum at contest depth, with trigonometry, complex numbers and advanced geometry that the AMC 10 leaves out
A fully worked original example in every fortnight, with the transferable idea written in one sentence
The 6, 1.5 and 0 scoring taught as real maths, so students know when a guess is worth more than a blank
Monthly 75-minute timed sets of original problems and an error log reviewed with the teacher
An AIME bridge built on the 2027 format: integer answers from 000 to 999, two parts of 8 and 7 questions, 90 minutes each, no return to Part 1
Honest by design: independent of the MAA, no copied contest problems, no promised scores or qualifications

phase_1_how_amc12_works_and_advanced_alg.title: PHASE 1: How the AMC 12 Works and Advanced Algebra (Months 1-2, Weeks 1-8)
phase_1_how_amc12_works_and_advanced_alg.description: Students learn the rules and scoring of the AMC 12, take a diagnostic, and build the advanced algebra that runs through the whole paper.

month_1_contest_rules_and_polynomials.title: Month 1: Contest Rules, Scoring Maths and Polynomials

week_1_2.title: Weeks 1-2: How the AMC 12 Works, Blank Versus Guess, and a Diagnostic
week_1_2.description: The AMC 12 gives 6 points for a right answer, 1.5 for a blank and 0 for a wrong one, so a blind guess is worth only 1.2 points on average and loses to leaving the question empty. Once two choices are ruled out, a guess among three is worth 2 points and beats the blank. The common trap is guessing everything out of habit from tests with no penalty, or leaving everything blank out of fear. This fortnight also sets a diagnostic so each student knows where to start.
topics: The format: 25 multiple-choice questions, five choices each, 75 minutes, no calculators
Eligibility: grade 12 or below and under 19.5 on competition day
The A and B dates, and why a student cannot sit the AMC 10 and AMC 12 on the same date
AMC 10 versus AMC 12: the trigonometry, advanced algebra and advanced geometry only the AMC 12 tests
Expected value of a guess: 6/5 with nothing ruled out, 6/4 with one ruled out, 6/3 with two ruled out
Elimination tactics: checking parity, sign, size and units against the choices
A diagnostic of our own across algebra, number theory, counting and geometry
Starting an error log: the question, the mistake, the fix, the idea to remember

worked_example.problem: A student finishes the AMC 12 sure of 15 answers, all of them correct. On 4 other questions she has ruled out exactly two choices each, and on the remaining 6 she has ruled out nothing. If she chooses for each group whether to guess or leave blank so as to make her expected score as large as possible, what is that expected score? (A) 101 (B) 104 (C) 105.5 (D) 107 (E) 110
steps: The 15 correct answers give 15 x 6 = 90 points.
On the 4 questions with three choices left, a guess is worth 6/3 = 2 points on average, more than 1.5 for a blank, so she guesses: 4 x 2 = 8.
On the 6 questions with five choices left, a guess is worth 6/5 = 1.2, less than 1.5, so she leaves them blank: 6 x 1.5 = 9.
Expected total: 90 + 8 + 9 = 107.
worked_example.idea: Guess only when you have ruled out at least two choices; otherwise the 1.5-point blank is worth more.

projects: A personal starting profile from the diagnostic: three strengths, three gaps and a first target list
week_1_2.practice: Ten original mixed problems in 25 minutes, with a blank-or-guess decision written beside each one left unfinished

week_3_4.title: Weeks 3-4: Polynomials, Vieta's Formulas, and the Remainder and Factor Theorems
week_3_4.description: Vieta's formulas link the roots of a polynomial to its coefficients, so you can find sums and products of roots without ever solving the equation. That matters because AMC 12 polynomials are often impossible to factor by hand, yet the question only asks about a symmetric expression of the roots. The trap is mixing up signs: for x^3 + ax^2 + bx + c the sum of roots is minus a, not a.
topics: Vieta's formulas for quadratics, cubics and quartics, with the sign pattern
Symmetric sums: sum of squares and sum of reciprocals of roots from the coefficients
The remainder theorem: P(a) is the remainder when P(x) is divided by x minus a
The factor theorem and finding integer roots with the rational root test
Polynomial division and the remainder on division by a quadratic
Building a polynomial from given roots, and transforming roots (roots doubled, roots shifted)
Counting real roots with sign changes and simple graph sketches
Coefficient sums: P(1) and P(-1) as quick checks

worked_example.problem: Let r, s and t be the roots of x^3 - 6x^2 + 5x - 2 = 0. What is r^2 + s^2 + t^2? (A) 16 (B) 21 (C) 26 (D) 31 (E) 36
steps: By Vieta, r + s + t = 6 and rs + st + tr = 5.
Use the identity r^2 + s^2 + t^2 = (r + s + t)^2 - 2(rs + st + tr).
worked_example.idea: When a question asks about a symmetric expression of roots, rewrite it in terms of sums and products and never solve the polynomial.

projects: A one-page polynomial formula sheet in the student's own words, with a tiny original example under each formula
week_3_4.practice: Twelve original polynomial problems in 30 minutes, each checked by substituting P(1) or a root back in
week_3_4.assessment: Month 1 check: a 40-minute timed set of original problems on scoring decisions and polynomials

month_2_functions_logs_and_series.title: Month 2: Functions, Exponentials, Logarithms, Sequences and Series

week_5_6.title: Weeks 5-6: Functions, Functional Reasoning, Exponentials and Logarithms
week_5_6.description: A logarithm answers the question: what power do I raise the base to? On the AMC 12 the key skill is changing every logarithm in a problem to one common base so they can be added like ordinary numbers. The usual trap is treating log_4 x as if it were log_2 x, forgetting that log_4 x is only half of log_2 x.
topics: Function notation, composition, inverses and domain restrictions
Functional equations solved by substituting clever values such as x and 1 - x
Laws of exponents and solving exponential equations by matching bases
Logarithm rules: product, quotient, power and change of base
Equations mixing logarithms of different bases
Checking that every solution is inside the domain of the logarithm
Comparing sizes of numbers like 2^100 and 3^63 using logarithms
Graphs of exponential and logarithmic functions and their transformations

worked_example.problem: If log_2 x + log_4 x + log_16 x = 7, what is x? (A) 2 (B) 4 (C) 8 (D) 16 (E) 32
steps: Change to base 2: log_4 x = (log_2 x)/2 and log_16 x = (log_2 x)/4.
The equation becomes log_2 x times (1 + 1/2 + 1/4) = 7, that is (7/4) log_2 x = 7.
So log_2 x = 4 and x = 2^4 = 16.
worked_example.idea: Put every logarithm in one base first; then the problem is ordinary algebra.

projects: An original set of six functional-equation and logarithm problems, each with a full solution written for a classmate
week_5_6.practice: Ten original problems in 25 minutes, with every answer checked against the domain

week_7_8.title: Weeks 7-8: Sequences, Series and Telescoping Sums
week_7_8.description: A telescoping sum is one where each term cancels part of the next, so a long sum collapses to its first and last pieces. The AMC 12 loves sums that look hopeless until one term is rewritten, often by rationalising a denominator or splitting a fraction. The trap is starting to add terms one by one and running out of time.
topics: Arithmetic sequences: nth term and sum formulas, and the average-times-count shortcut
Geometric sequences and infinite geometric series with ratio between minus 1 and 1
Telescoping by partial fractions such as 1/(k(k+1)) = 1/k - 1/(k+1)
Telescoping by rationalising denominators with square roots
Recursive sequences: computing early terms and spotting a cycle
Sums of squares and cubes and when to use them
Sigma notation read and rewritten correctly

worked_example.problem: What is the value of the sum 1/(sqrt(1) + sqrt(2)) + 1/(sqrt(2) + sqrt(3)) + ... + 1/(sqrt(24) + sqrt(25))? (A) 3 (B) 4 (C) 5 (D) 2 sqrt(6) (E) 24
steps: Rationalise one term: 1/(sqrt(k) + sqrt(k+1)) = (sqrt(k+1) - sqrt(k)) / ((k+1) - k) = sqrt(k+1) - sqrt(k).
The sum becomes (sqrt(2) - sqrt(1)) + (sqrt(3) - sqrt(2)) + ... + (sqrt(25) - sqrt(24)).
Everything in the middle cancels, leaving sqrt(25) - sqrt(1) = 5 - 1 = 4.
worked_example.idea: If a long sum appears, rewrite one general term as a difference and look for cancellation before adding anything.

projects: A series toolkit page: arithmetic, geometric and three telescoping patterns, each with an original example
week_7_8.practice: Eight original series problems in 20 minutes, writing the general term before any arithmetic
week_7_8.assessment: Phase 1 assessment: a 75-minute timed set of 25 original problems on scoring, polynomials, functions, logarithms and series, scored 6, 1.5 and 0

phase_2_trigonometry_complex_numbers_num.title: PHASE 2: Trigonometry, Complex Numbers and Number Theory (Months 3-4, Weeks 9-16)
phase_2_trigonometry_complex_numbers_num.description: The topics that separate the AMC 12 from the AMC 10: trigonometry and complex numbers, followed by number theory at the depth the hardest questions need.

week_9_10.title: Weeks 9-10: Trigonometric Identities, the Law of Sines and the Law of Cosines
week_9_10.description: The law of cosines is the Pythagorean theorem for any triangle: it gives an angle from three sides, or a side from two sides and the angle between them. Once an angle is known, the area is half of two sides times the sine of the angle between them. The trap is using the wrong angle: the angle in the formula must sit opposite the side you single out.
topics: Unit circle values for multiples of 30 and 45 degrees, known by heart
Pythagorean, double-angle and sum and difference identities
The law of sines, including the circumradius form a/sin A = 2R
The law of cosines for finding angles and sides
Triangle area as (1/2)ab sin C
Trigonometry inside geometry: heights, chords and inscribed angles
Solving trigonometric equations on a stated interval
Radians and degrees, and converting without slips

worked_example.problem: A triangle has sides 5, 7 and 8. What is its area? (A) 10 (B) 10 sqrt(2) (C) 10 sqrt(3) (D) 20 (E) 20 sqrt(3)
steps: Let C be the angle opposite the side 7. By the law of cosines, 49 = 25 + 64 - 2(5)(8) cos C.
So 80 cos C = 40 and cos C = 1/2, which gives C = 60 degrees.
Area = (1/2)(5)(8) sin 60 degrees = 20 x (sqrt(3)/2) = 10 sqrt(3).
Check with Heron's formula: s = 10 and sqrt(10 x 5 x 3 x 2) = sqrt(300) = 10 sqrt(3).
worked_example.idea: Use the law of cosines to find a nice angle, then the sine area formula finishes the job.

projects: A trigonometry reference card written from memory: unit circle values, the key identities and both laws
week_9_10.practice: Ten original trigonometry problems in 25 minutes, each with a labelled sketch

week_11_12.title: Weeks 11-12: Complex Numbers, Polar Form, De Moivre and Roots of Unity
week_11_12.description: A complex number can be written by its distance from zero and its angle, and in that form multiplying means multiply the distances and add the angles. That turns a huge power like (1 + i)^20 into a quick calculation. The trap is expanding the power by hand, which takes far too long and invites mistakes.
topics: Rectangular form, conjugates and modulus
Polar form r(cos t + i sin t) and converting between forms
De Moivre's theorem for powers
The nth roots of unity as vertices of a regular polygon
Sums and products of roots of unity, and why they are often 0 or 1
Complex numbers as rotations in the plane
Solving z^n = w for all n solutions
Using complex numbers to evaluate trigonometric sums

steps: Write 1 + i in polar form: modulus sqrt(2), angle 45 degrees.
By De Moivre, (1 + i)^20 has modulus (sqrt(2))^20 = 2^10 = 1024 and angle 20 x 45 = 900 degrees.
900 degrees is 2 full turns plus 180 degrees, so the number points along the negative real axis.
worked_example.idea: For powers of complex numbers, switch to modulus and angle; powers become multiplication and addition.

projects: A diagram sheet of the 6th, 8th and 12th roots of unity with three original questions about each
week_11_12.practice: Eight original complex-number problems in 20 minutes, with the polar form written first
week_11_12.assessment: Month 3 check: a 45-minute timed set of original trigonometry and complex-number problems

week_13_14.title: Weeks 13-14: Modular Arithmetic and Orders
week_13_14.description: Modular arithmetic means keeping only the remainder, like reading a clock. To find the last two digits of a huge power you only need the remainder when dividing by 100, and powers always fall into a repeating cycle. The trap is trying to compute the power itself instead of finding how long the cycle is.
topics: Congruences and the rules for adding, subtracting and multiplying them
Last digits and last two digits of large powers
The order of a number: the smallest power that gives remainder 1
Fermat's little theorem and Euler's theorem as shortcuts for the cycle length
Divisibility tests proved with modular arithmetic
Solving linear congruences and finding inverses
Squares modulo 3, 4, 8 and 9 to rule out impossible equations

worked_example.problem: What is the remainder when 7^2026 is divided by 100? (A) 1 (B) 7 (C) 43 (D) 49 (E) 57
steps: Compute small powers mod 100: 7^1 = 7, 7^2 = 49, 7^3 = 343, which is 43 mod 100, and 7^4 = 2401, which is 1 mod 100.
So the order of 7 mod 100 is 4: the remainders repeat every 4 powers.
2026 = 4 x 506 + 2, so 7^2026 has the same remainder as 7^2.
The remainder is 49.
worked_example.idea: For a huge power, find the cycle length first, then reduce the exponent by that length.

projects: An order table of our own: the order of 2, 3, 7 and 9 modulo 10, 100 and 13, with the pattern explained
week_13_14.practice: Ten original modular-arithmetic problems in 25 minutes, no calculator

week_15_16.title: Weeks 15-16: The Chinese Remainder Idea, Divisors and Bases
week_15_16.description: The Chinese remainder idea says that if you know a number's remainders when divided by numbers that share no factors, the number is fixed up to their product. In practice you solve one condition, list the numbers that satisfy it, and test them against the next condition. The trap is listing all numbers up to the product one by one when stepping through a single condition is far faster.
topics: Systems of congruences solved by stepping through one condition at a time
Why the moduli must share no common factor for a unique answer
Prime factorisation and the formulas for the number and sum of divisors
GCD, LCM and the Euclidean algorithm
Number bases: converting, and arithmetic in base b
Digit problems written as polynomials in the base
Diophantine equations solved with factoring and parity

worked_example.problem: What is the smallest positive integer that leaves remainder 2 when divided by 5, remainder 3 when divided by 7, and remainder 4 when divided by 9? (A) 67 (B) 112 (C) 157 (D) 202 (E) 247
steps: Remainder 4 on division by 9 means the number is one of 4, 13, 22, 31, 40, 49, 58, 67, 76, 85, 94, 103, 112, 121, 130, 139, 148, 157, and so on.
Remainder 3 on division by 7 picks out 31, then every 63 after it: 31, 94, 157, 220, and so on.
Check remainder 2 on division by 5: 31 gives 1, 94 gives 4, 157 gives 2.
The answer is 157, and the next one would be 157 + 315 = 472.
worked_example.idea: Satisfy one congruence, then step in jumps of its modulus to meet the next; the answers repeat every product of the moduli.

projects: Write five original number-theory problems with full solutions for a newer student
week_15_16.practice: Ten original number-theory problems in 25 minutes, each answer checked against every condition
week_15_16.assessment: Phase 2 assessment: a 75-minute timed set of 25 original problems on trigonometry, complex numbers and number theory, scored 6, 1.5 and 0

phase_3_counting_probability_geometry.title: PHASE 3: Counting, Probability and Advanced Geometry (Months 5-6, Weeks 17-24)
phase_3_counting_probability_geometry.description: Counting and probability at AMC 12 level, then the advanced geometry the senior contest tests: circles, coordinates, vectors, solids and areas through trigonometry.

week_17_18.title: Weeks 17-18: Combinatorial Identities and Recursion
week_17_18.description: Recursion means counting the big case by building it from smaller cases you have already counted. For example, a string with no two 1s next to each other either ends in 0 or ends in 01, which links each length to the two before it. The trap is trying to list every case directly, which is slow and almost always misses some.
topics: Permutations, combinations and the multiplication principle
Stars and bars for distributing identical objects
Pascal's identity and the hockey stick identity
Complementary counting and inclusion-exclusion
Setting up a recursion from the last step
Fibonacci-type recursions in tilings, stairs and strings
Bijections: counting one set by matching it with an easier one
Counting with symmetry and avoiding double counting

worked_example.problem: How many strings of ten digits, each digit 0 or 1, contain no two 1s next to each other? (A) 55 (B) 89 (C) 110 (D) 144 (E) 233
steps: Let a(n) be the number of good strings of length n. A good string either ends in 0, after any good string of length n - 1, or ends in 01, after any good string of length n - 2.
So a(n) = a(n - 1) + a(n - 2), with a(1) = 2 and a(2) = 3.
worked_example.idea: Split by how the object ends; that usually gives a recursion you can run in under a minute.

projects: A recursion notebook page: three original counting problems, each solved once by recursion and once by another method
week_17_18.practice: Ten original counting problems in 25 minutes, with the method named before solving

week_19_20.title: Weeks 19-20: Expected Value and Conditional Probability
week_19_20.description: Conditional probability asks for a chance when you already know something has happened, so the known event becomes the whole new set of possibilities. Expected value is the long-run average, and linearity of expectation lets you add expected values even when events depend on each other. The trap is dividing by all 36 dice outcomes when the question has already told you which smaller set you are in.
topics: Probability as favourable over equally likely outcomes, and when outcomes are not equally likely
Conditional probability: restrict to the known event, then count
Independence, and checking it rather than assuming it
Expected value as a weighted average
Linearity of expectation with indicator variables
Geometric probability using lengths and areas
States and simple recursions for games and random walks

worked_example.problem: Two fair six-sided dice are rolled and the sum is 8. What is the probability that at least one die shows a 6? (A) 1/6 (B) 11/36 (C) 1/3 (D) 2/5 (E) 1/2
steps: List the outcomes with sum 8: (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3), (6,2). There are 5, all equally likely.
The ones with a 6 are (2,6) and (6,2): 2 outcomes.
The probability is 2/5.
worked_example.idea: Given information shrinks the sample space; count only inside the event you are told has happened.

projects: An expected-value experiment: simulate an original game by hand 30 times, then compare with the exact expected value
week_19_20.practice: Ten original probability problems in 25 minutes, each with the sample space written first
week_19_20.assessment: Month 5 check: a 45-minute timed set of original counting and probability problems

week_21_22.title: Weeks 21-22: Circles and Power of a Point
week_21_22.description: Power of a point says that for any line through a point and a circle, the product of the two distances from the point to the circle is always the same number. For a tangent, both distances are the tangent length, so the product is the tangent length squared. The trap is multiplying the inside piece of a secant instead of the whole distance from the point.
topics: Inscribed angles, central angles and cyclic quadrilaterals
Power of a point for two chords, two secants and a tangent with a secant
Tangent lengths from an external point being equal
Incircle and circumcircle radii, including area = rs and R = abc/(4K)
Ptolemy's theorem for cyclic quadrilaterals
Similar triangles hidden inside circle diagrams
Choosing between synthetic, trigonometric and coordinate approaches

worked_example.problem: From a point P outside a circle, a tangent touches the circle at T with PT = 12. A line through P meets the circle at A and then at B, with PA = 8. What is AB? (A) 9 (B) 10 (C) 12 (D) 15 (E) 18
steps: Power of a point: PA x PB = PT^2.
So 8 x PB = 144, which gives PB = 18.
worked_example.idea: Every distance in power of a point is measured from the point itself, so find the whole secant first, then subtract.

projects: A circle theorems poster with one original diagram and problem for each theorem
week_21_22.practice: Eight original circle problems in 25 minutes, each with an accurate diagram drawn first

week_23_24.title: Weeks 23-24: Coordinates, Vectors, Three-Dimensional Solids and Areas via Trigonometry
week_23_24.description: Many hard geometry questions become routine once you place the figure on coordinate axes, because lengths, planes and distances turn into short formulas. A cube is ideal for this, since its corners have simple coordinates. The trap is placing the axes awkwardly, which makes every later step messy.
topics: Placing a figure on axes to keep the algebra small
Distance, midpoint and section formulas in two and three dimensions
Vectors, dot products and the angle between two lines
Equation of a plane and distance from a point to a plane
Volumes and surface areas of prisms, pyramids, cylinders, cones and spheres
Cross sections and nets of solids
Areas of polygons using trigonometry and the shoelace formula

worked_example.problem: A cube has edge length 6. One vertex is V, and the three vertices joined to V by an edge determine a plane. What is the distance from V to that plane? (A) sqrt(3) (B) 2 sqrt(2) (C) 3 (D) 2 sqrt(3) (E) 3 sqrt(2)
steps: Put V at (0, 0, 0); its three neighbours are (6, 0, 0), (0, 6, 0) and (0, 0, 6).
Those three points lie on the plane x + y + z = 6.
The distance from (0, 0, 0) to that plane is |0 + 0 + 0 - 6| / sqrt(1 + 1 + 1) = 6/sqrt(3).
Simplify: 6/sqrt(3) = 2 sqrt(3).
worked_example.idea: Choose coordinates that make the given points simple; a plane through intercepts a, a, a is x + y + z = a.

projects: A geometry method map: one original problem solved three ways (synthetic, trigonometric, coordinates), with a note on which was quickest
week_23_24.practice: Eight original coordinate and solid-geometry problems in 25 minutes
week_23_24.assessment: Phase 3 assessment: a 75-minute timed set of 25 original problems on counting, probability and geometry, scored 6, 1.5 and 0

phase_4_contest_craft_and_aime_bridge.title: PHASE 4: Contest Craft and the AIME Bridge (Months 7-8, Weeks 25-32)
phase_4_contest_craft_and_aime_bridge.description: Full-length 75-minute practice, pacing and error review for the AMC 12, then a bridge to the 2027 AIME with integer answers and the new two-part format.

week_25_26.title: Weeks 25-26: Pacing, Estimation and Using the Answer Choices
week_25_26.description: Pacing means deciding in advance how long each part of the paper deserves, so the hard questions at the end get real time. Estimation is a big part of this: often you only need to know which answer is largest, not its exact value. The trap is spending ten minutes on one early question and arriving at the last ten with no time left.
topics: A 75-minute plan: a first pass on the early questions, then the middle, then the hardest
Recognising in under a minute whether a problem is for now, later or blank
Estimation with logarithms and bounds to compare answer choices
Testing simple cases and plugging in choices when that is faster
Reading the choices first to see what form the answer takes
Checking with parity, size and special values before committing
The blank-or-guess rule applied in real time

worked_example.problem: Which of these numbers is the largest? (A) 10^30 (B) 5^43 (C) 3^63 (D) 2^100 (E) 7^36
steps: Compare the base 10 logarithms: log 2 is about 0.301, log 3 about 0.477, log 5 about 0.699, log 7 about 0.845.
Estimates: 10^30 gives 30, 5^43 gives about 30.06, 3^63 about 30.06, 2^100 about 30.10, and 7^36 about 30.42.
The others are all very close to 30, but 7^36 is clearly larger.
The gap is safe: 30.42 against 30.10 means 7^36 is about twice 2^100, far bigger than any rounding error in the estimates.
worked_example.idea: When choices are huge powers, compare their logarithms; a rough estimate is enough to separate them.

worked_example.problem: How many ordered pairs of integers (x, y) satisfy x^2 - y^2 = 2026? (A) 0 (B) 2 (C) 4 (D) 8 (E) 16
steps: Factor: x^2 - y^2 = (x - y)(x + y).
x - y and x + y differ by 2y, an even number, so they are both even or both odd.
If both are odd, the product is odd. If both are even, the product is a multiple of 4.
2026 is even but 2026 = 4 x 506 + 2, so it is not a multiple of 4. No pair works.
worked_example.idea: Before searching for solutions, check remainders mod 2 or mod 4; the answer may be none.

week_29_30.title: Weeks 29-30: How the 2027 AIME Works and Integer-Answer Problems
week_29_30.description: From 2027, the AIME is open to students who score 85 or more on the AMC 12, plus other eligibility rules. It has 15 questions with no answer choices, and every answer is an integer from 000 to 999, so you cannot check against choices or guess usefully. The trap is stopping at an answer that is close but not finished, for example forgetting to take the remainder the question asks for.

Why integer answers change checking: no choices to test

worked_example.problem: AIME style, answer an integer from 000 to 999: let S be the sum of all positive divisors of 360. Find the remainder when S is divided by 1000.
steps: The divisor sum multiplies across prime powers: (1 + 2 + 4 + 8)(1 + 3 + 9)(1 + 5) = 15 x 13 x 6.
1170 divided by 1000 leaves remainder 170.
worked_example.idea: On integer-answer problems, finish the last step the question asks for, such as the remainder, before you write the answer.

worked_example.problem: AIME style, answer an integer from 000 to 999: for how many integers n with 1 <= n <= 999 is (1 + i)^n a real number?
steps: (1 + i) has angle 45 degrees, so (1 + i)^n has angle 45n degrees.
It is real exactly when 45n is a multiple of 180, that is when n is a multiple of 4.
The multiples of 4 from 1 to 999 are 4, 8, ..., 996.
There are 996/4 = 249 of them.
worked_example.idea: Turn a condition about complex powers into a condition about angles, then count with divisibility.

faqs.question: What is the AMC 12?
faqs.answer: The AMC 12 is a high school mathematics contest run by the Mathematical Association of America (MAA), the senior contest in the American Mathematics Competitions after the AMC 8 and AMC 10. It has 25 multiple-choice questions in 75 minutes, with no calculators. It covers the whole high school curriculum, including trigonometry, advanced algebra and advanced geometry, but no calculus.

faqs.question: How is the AMC 12 scored?
faqs.answer: Each correct answer earns 6 points, each blank earns 1.5 points and each wrong answer earns 0, for a maximum of 150. Because a blank earns points, guessing has a cost. A random guess among five choices is worth 1.2 points on average, less than a blank, while a guess after ruling out two choices is worth 2 points, more than a blank.

faqs.question: Should my child guess or leave questions blank?
faqs.answer: It depends on how many choices they can rule out. With none ruled out, leave it blank (1.2 points expected versus 1.5). With one ruled out it is break-even at 1.5, and with two or more ruled out a guess is worth more. We practise this decision on every timed set so it becomes quick.

faqs.question: Who can take the AMC 12?
faqs.answer: Students in grade 12 or below who are under 19.5 years old on competition day. Younger students can take it too if they are ready for the content. The MAA's current rules always take priority, so check them with your school or competition manager.

faqs.question: How do we register, and when is it held?
faqs.answer: Registration is done through a school or an approved competition manager, not through us. The contest runs twice a year as the AMC 12A and AMC 12B; in 2026 the dates were 5 November and 13 November. A student may sit one A and one B contest, but not the AMC 10 and AMC 12 on the same date.

faqs.question: Should my child take the AMC 10 or the AMC 12?
faqs.answer: The AMC 10 is for grade 10 or below and stops at elementary algebra, basic geometry, elementary number theory and elementary probability. The AMC 12 adds trigonometry, advanced algebra and advanced geometry. A student in grade 10 or below who is comfortable with trigonometry and complex numbers may prefer the AMC 12; others often start with the AMC 10, and we have a separate AMC 10 course. The teacher can advise after the free demo class.

faqs.question: What changed for the 2027 AIME?
faqs.answer: The MAA announced on 26 August 2026 that AIME qualification is now a fixed score: 85 or more on the AMC 12, or 100 or more on the AMC 10, plus other eligibility rules. The 2027 AIME is 15 questions with integer answers from 000 to 999, taken on computer at Pearson testing centers in the US and Canada on 5 or 6 February 2027. It has two parts, 8 questions in 90 minutes and then 7 questions in 90 minutes, and you cannot return to Part 1. Students must be at least 13, and the fee is $85 plus taxes.

faqs.question: How are USAJMO and USAMO students selected now?
faqs.answer: Selection is now primarily based on the AIME score, and AMC scores are no longer a factor. That makes the AIME bridge in Month 8 important for students aiming beyond the AMC 12. Our course stops at the AIME bridge; olympiad proof writing is covered in our separate year-long olympiad course.

faqs.question: We live outside the US and Canada. Does this still apply?
faqs.answer: The mathematics is the same wherever you live, and the course works the same online. For which AMC and AIME rules apply to students outside the US and Canada, check with your competition manager what applies to you.

faqs.question: When should my child start?
faqs.answer: The course is eight months, so starting in the spring or early summer leaves time to finish before the November contest dates. Students can join any month, and a later start still gives months of timed practice. In the free demo class the teacher looks at your child's level and suggests a start date.

faqs.question: What does a class look like?
faqs.answer: Each live class introduces one idea, works through an original example step by step, then gives students problems to try while the teacher watches and helps. There are two one-hour classes a week, a problem set after each class and a timed set every month. Classes run in group batches of 15 to 20 students or 1-on-1.

faqs.question: How is this different from your year-long olympiad course?
faqs.answer: Our olympiad course runs for more than a year and leads from the AMC through the AIME towards olympiad proof writing. This course is only the AMC 12: eight months on the exact high school content, scoring and pacing of the AMC 12, a worked example in every fortnight, and an AIME bridge at the end. Students who finish here and want proofs can move on to the olympiad course.

faqs.question: Do you use real AMC problems?
faqs.answer: No. Every problem in our materials is original and written by us at contest level. Past AMC papers are published by the MAA, and students may practise with them on their own, but we never copy or reconstruct contest items.

faqs.question: Can you guarantee an AIME qualification or a score?
faqs.answer: No. We are independent of the MAA and promise learning, never scores, AIME qualification or awards. What we do promise is live teaching, original problems, monthly timed sets, an error log and honest feedback on every weak topic.
